বিভাগ 3 স্তনের স্বাস্থ্য আপনার স্তন বোঝা: পরিবর্তন, যত্ন এবং আত্মবিশ্বাস।
বিভাগ 4 ত্বকের স্বাস্থ্য এবং হরমোন আপনার ত্বক কথা বলে। এটি যা বলে তা বোঝা সবকিছু বদলে দেয়।
বিভাগ 5 অন্তরঙ্গ স্বাস্থ্যহীনতা আরও বেশি। সৌম্য ভালো। শরীর নিজেকে পরিষ্কার করতে জানে।

পর্যায় 1: মাসিক। জরায়ু তিন থেকে সাত দিনের মধ্যে তার আস্তরণ ফেলে দেয়। এই সময়কাল। পর্যায় 2: ফলিকুলার ফেজ। ইস্ট্রোজেন বেড়ে যায়। ডিম্বাশয়ের একটি ফলিকল একটি ডিম প্রস্তুত করে। জরায়ু একটি নতুন আস্তরণ তৈরি করে। পর্যায় 3: ডিম্বস্ফোটন। ডিম্বাশয় থেকে ডিম্বাণু বের হয়। এটি সবচেয়ে উর্বর সময়। পর্যায় 4: লুটেল ফেজ। প্রোজেস্টেরন বেড়ে যায়। গর্ভাবস্থা না ঘটলে, হরমোনের মাত্রা কমে যায়। চক্র আবার শুরু হয়।
বিভাগ 6 স্রাব এবং যৌনাঙ্গে সংক্রমণ জ্ঞান ভয় দূর করে। তথ্য সঠিক প্রতিক্রিয়া গাইড.

বিভাগ 8 পিরিয়ড, ব্যথা, এবং PCOS প্রতিটি কোণ থেকে মাসিক স্বাস্থ্য বোঝা।
বিভাগ 9 থাইরয়েড, অ্যানিমিয়া, এবং হরমোনজনিত স্বাস্থ্যদুটি খুব সাধারণ অবস্থা যা অল্পবয়সী মহিলাদেরকে নীরবে এবং গভীরভাবে প্রভাবিত করে৷
অনুচ্ছেদ 10আবেগজনিত স্বাস্থ্য, জীবনধারা, এবং বিশেষ বিষয় সমগ্র মহিলার যত্ন নেওয়া: মন, শরীর এবং দৈনন্দিন অভ্যাস।
অনুচ্ছেদ 11 বিবাহ, গর্ভাবস্থা এবং প্রসবোত্তর স্বাস্থ্য একজন মহিলার প্রজনন জীবনের প্রতিটি পর্যায়ে সম্মান, বোঝাপড়া এবং ভাল যত্নের যোগ্য।
বিভাগ 14 সাধারণ মহিলাদের স্বাস্থ্যের অবস্থা ওভারিয়ান সিস্ট, ফাইব্রয়েড, এন্ডোমেট্রিওসিস, পিএমএস, পিএমডিডি, এবং হরমোনের ভারসাম্যহীনতা।
বিভাগ 15মেডিকেল কেয়ার এবং মহিলাদের চেক-আপ গাইনোকোলজিক্যাল কেয়ার হল প্রতিরোধমূলক যত্ন। প্রাথমিক পরিদর্শন দীর্ঘমেয়াদী স্বাস্থ্য রক্ষা করে।

দাবিত্যাগ

এই বইটি শুধুমাত্র শিক্ষা এবং সাধারণ সচেতনতার জন্য। এটি একজন যোগ্যতাসম্পন্ন ডাক্তারের পরামর্শ প্রতিস্থাপন করে না। আপনার ব্যক্তিগত স্বাস্থ্যের প্রয়োজনের জন্য সর্বদা একজন স্বাস্থ্যসেবা পেশাদারের সাথে পরামর্শ করুন। একা এই বইয়ের উপর ভিত্তি করে কখনও স্ব-নির্ণয় বা স্ব-ঔষধ করবেন না।

স্বাস্থ্য সখি থেকে একটি নোট

এই বই আপনার জন্য লেখা হয়েছে. প্রতিটি মেয়ের জন্য যাদের একটি প্রশ্ন ছিল কিন্তু জিজ্ঞাসা করতে খুব লজ্জা বোধ করে। প্রতিটি যুবতীর জন্য যারা তার শরীরের পরিবর্তন লক্ষ্য করেছে এবং জানে না যে এটি স্বাভাবিক কিনা। প্রতিটি কন্যার জন্য যাদের সহজ, সৎ, সম্মানজনক উত্তর প্রয়োজন।

এই বইয়ের প্রতিটি অধ্যায় একটি বাস্তব ঘটনা দিয়ে শুরু হয়। এগুলো তোমার মত মেয়েদের গল্প। মেয়েরা যারা চিন্তিত, বিস্মিত এবং অবশেষে শিখেছে। তাদের নাম আলাদা। কিন্তু তাদের অনুভূতি আপনার।

ধীরে ধীরে পড়ুন। আপনার যা প্রয়োজন তা পড়ুন। এই বইটি বিচার করে না। এটা শুধুমাত্র যত্ন করে.

Chapter 1

Understanding the Female Body

Every girl deserves to know her own body

Riya, 17 — School student

Riya hears many things about the female body from friends, social media, and relatives. Some things sound scary. Some things sound confusing. She notices her body changing and wonders if everything is normal. She feels shy to ask questions at home.

The female body is not confusing. It is organized. It follows a pattern. Every part has a purpose. Knowing your body is not shameful. It is the first step toward taking care of yourself.

The Body Has Two Kinds of Parts

External parts are the ones visible from outside. Internal parts work quietly inside the body. They manage periods, hormones, and fertility. Both kinds of parts start becoming more active after puberty.

What Are Hormones?

Hormones are chemical messengers. They travel through the blood and tell different parts of the body what to do. They tell the body when to grow. They tell the body when periods should start. They also affect mood, skin, sleep, and energy.

Every Girl's Timing Is Different

Some girls develop early. Some develop later. Both are completely normal. The body follows its own schedule. There is no right age or wrong age for these changes to begin.

"Knowing your body makes you confident and careful. It is knowledge, not boldness."

💮

Chapter 2

External Genital Anatomy Explained Simply

Understanding the outer private area

Kavya, 18 — College student

Kavya feels mild irritation around her private area. She panics and washes repeatedly. The irritation increases. She had never been taught what this area of her body looks like or how to care for it.

The outer private area is called the vulva. It includes the outer skin folds and the opening area. This skin is very sensitive. It protects the inner parts of the body.

What Does the Vulva Include?

The vulva has two sets of skin folds. Outer folds are called labia majora. Inner folds are called labia minora. There is also a small area at the top where a sensitive spot is located. Below that is the opening of the urethra, where urine comes out. Further below is the genital opening.

Every Vulva Looks Different

Size, color, and shape vary between every woman. One side may look different from the other. This is completely normal. There is no perfect shape. Images online often show edited or altered pictures. Do not compare your body with those.

Simple Care for the Vulva

• Wash with plain water from front to back

• Use mild unscented soap only on the outer skin folds if needed

• Avoid strong soaps, sprays, or scented products

• Wear cotton innerwear to keep the area dry

• Change innerwear daily

"Irritation is often caused by harsh products or tight clothing, not by being dirty. Gentle care is the best care."

🫀

Chapter 3

Internal Genital Anatomy Made Easy

Understanding what works inside

Sara, 20 — College student

Sara knows words like uterus and ovaries from biology class. But she does not know what these organs actually do. She feels confused and a little afraid of her own body.

The internal reproductive organs work quietly inside the body every day. Understanding what they do removes confusion and fear.

The Uterus

Sugar and refined carbohydrates cause a rapid spike in blood glucose. The body responds by releasing large amounts of insulin. When this pattern repeats daily, the cells become less sensitive to insulin, requiring the body to produce ever more of it. This state is called insulin resistance.

Why Insulin Resistance Matters for Women

Insulin resistance drives PCOS, worsens acne, promotes weight gain particularly around the abdomen, disrupts the menstrual cycle, increases PMS symptoms, and raises long-term risk of type 2 diabetes. It also drives the darkening of skin on the neck and underarms. Reducing sugar and refined carbohydrates is therefore one of the most important dietary changes a woman with any of these concerns can make.

• Replace white rice with brown rice, millets like jowar and bajra, or quinoa

• Replace white bread with whole grain bread or rotis

• Replace sugary drinks with water, buttermilk, or unsweetened herbal teas

• Replace packaged snacks with nuts, seeds, fruit with protein, or homemade snacks

• Reduce sugar in tea and coffee gradually rather than eliminating at once

• Read labels: products labeled as healthy often contain high sugar

"Sugar is not forbidden. But in the amounts that modern food systems provide it, it quietly disrupts the hormonal balance that your health depends on. Gradual reduction creates lasting benefit."

Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder — PMDD

When premenstrual symptoms become seriously disruptive

Every month in the week before her period, Leena's world turns dark. She becomes deeply sad. She cannot concentrate at work. She feels hopeless for no reason she can name. Small disagreements feel devastating. She cannot sleep properly. As soon as her period begins, the darkness lifts completely. She has been told for years that this is just PMS. It is not. It is PMDD.

Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder, or PMDD, is a severe form of premenstrual syndrome that causes significant emotional, psychological, and physical symptoms in the week or two before a period. Unlike PMS which causes manageable discomfort, PMDD causes symptoms severe enough to disrupt work, relationships, and daily functioning.

How PMDD Differs From PMS

PMS causes common premenstrual symptoms like bloating, breast tenderness, mild mood changes, and irritability. These are uncomfortable but manageable. PMDD involves severe depression, intense anxiety or panic, extreme irritability or anger, feelings of hopelessness, difficulty concentrating, marked fatigue, significant changes in appetite or sleep, and a sense of being overwhelmed. The critical feature of PMDD is that these symptoms resolve significantly within a few days of the period starting. They follow the hormonal cycle precisely.

Recognizing PMDD Symptoms

• Marked depression or hopelessness in the premenstrual phase

• Anxiety or tension that feels unmanageable

• Sudden and intense irritability or anger that damages relationships

• Marked mood swings, crying without clear reason

• Difficulty concentrating and reduced efficiency at work or study

• Significant fatigue and low energy

• Changes in appetite including cravings or loss of appetite

• Sleep disturbance: too much or too little sleep

• Feeling out of control or overwhelmed

• Physical symptoms including breast tenderness, bloating, headaches

• All symptoms begin to resolve when the period starts

What Causes PMDD

PMDD is caused by an abnormal sensitivity of the brain's mood-regulating systems to the normal hormonal fluctuations of the menstrual cycle. Estrogen and progesterone change throughout the cycle for all women. In PMDD, the brain reacts to these changes with an exaggerated emotional and neurological response. It is not a character weakness. It is a biological vulnerability of the brain's chemistry.

WHAT SCIENCE SAYS · PMDD and Serotonin

Research shows that PMDD is linked to altered serotonin system sensitivity. Progesterone, which rises after ovulation and falls sharply before periods, affects serotonin pathways in the brain. In women with PMDD, this effect is amplified. This is why treatments that support serotonin function, including certain antidepressants used cyclically, are among the most effective treatments for PMDD.

How PMDD Is Diagnosed

• PMDD is diagnosed by tracking symptoms across at least two menstrual cycles

• A daily symptom diary or app showing the cyclical pattern confirms the diagnosis

• Symptoms must be present in the premenstrual phase and resolve after the period begins

• The symptoms must cause significant disruption to work, relationships, or daily life

• A doctor rules out depression, anxiety disorder, and thyroid problems before diagnosing PMDD

Managing PMDD

• Lifestyle: regular aerobic exercise significantly reduces PMDD severity. Consistent sleep is essential.

• Nutrition: reducing caffeine, sugar, and alcohol in the premenstrual phase reduces symptom severity

• Stress management: evidence-based techniques including CBT are effective for PMDD

• Medical support: SSRIs (a type of antidepressant) used either continuously or only in the premenstrual phase are the most studied medical treatment

• Hormonal options: certain contraceptive methods can reduce hormonal fluctuation and improve PMDD

• Nutritional supplements: calcium, magnesium, and vitamin B6 have evidence supporting modest benefit

WHEN TO SEE A DOCTOR

• Thoughts of self-harm or suicide during the premenstrual phase require immediate mental health support

• If PMDD significantly affects work, relationships, or quality of life for more than two consecutive cycles, seek medical evaluation

• Do not dismiss severe premenstrual mental health symptoms as normal

"PMDD is a recognized medical condition. It is not weakness, drama, or a difficult personality. It is a brain that responds strongly to normal hormonal changes. It is diagnosable and treatable."

• A compassionate, non-judgmental doctor or counselor is the right starting point

Genital Hair: Shaving, Grooming, and Complete Care

Everything you need to know, without the pressure

Rania, 20 — College student

Rania has been removing her pubic hair since she was seventeen because she believed it was necessary for hygiene. She has never been told otherwise. After her third case of folliculitis (infected hair follicles) in a year, a doctor explains that her removal method is causing repeated infections, and that she does not need to remove the hair at all.

Genital hair, called pubic hair or intimate area hair, serves genuine biological functions. It reduces friction between skin surfaces during movement, traps moisture away from the delicate genital skin, provides a minor physical barrier, and may play a role in natural scent communication. Removing it is entirely a personal choice. It is not a hygiene requirement. No medical authority recommends pubic hair removal for health reasons.

The Pressure to Remove

Media, social media, and some intimate product advertisements have created a culture in which bare genital skin is presented as the cleaner or more desirable option. This is a social and commercial construction, not a medical fact. Many women report discomfort, infections, ingrown hairs, and skin irritation as direct results of hair removal practices they undertook because of social pressure rather than personal preference.

Leaving Hair: The Simplest Option

Leaving genital hair unremoved requires no maintenance, carries no infection risk, and is the biologically natural state. If this is your preference, it is a completely healthy choice that requires only ordinary hygiene: gentle washing with water and mild soap of the outer area.

Trimming: The Safest Active Choice

Trimming reduces hair length without contact with the skin. It avoids the risks associated with shaving, waxing, and chemical creams. Use small, clean scissors or a dedicated electric trimmer with a guard attachment. Never trim on irritated, broken, or infected skin. Clean the tool before and after use.

Shaving: Safe Practices

Shaving is the most commonly used hair removal method but carries the highest risk of problems in the genital area. The skin here is thinner, more sensitive, and has more hair follicles than other body areas.

How to Shave Safely in the Genital Area

• Use a new, clean, sharp razor each time. Blunt blades cause cuts and razor burn

• Never shave dry skin. Wet the area thoroughly with warm water for at least two minutes first

• Apply an unscented, fragrance-free shaving gel or cream. Never use scented products

• Shave slowly in the direction of hair growth, not against it

• Use single gentle strokes without pressing hard into the skin

• Rinse the area with cool water after shaving to close pores

• Pat dry gently with a clean cloth. Do not rub

• Wear loose cotton underwear for 24-48 hours after shaving to allow skin to settle

• Do not apply deodorant, perfume, or scented products to freshly shaved skin

• Replace the razor after every 2-3 uses in this area

Problems to Watch for After Shaving

• Razor burn: redness and irritation immediately after shaving. Resolves with cool water and time

• Folliculitis: red, pimple-like bumps around hair follicles caused by bacteria entering shaved skin. Needs gentle care and sometimes antifungal or antibiotic cream

• Ingrown hairs: hairs that curl back into the skin causing bumps and sometimes infection. Warm compress and gentle exfoliation help prevention

• Cuts: small nicks from the blade. Apply gentle pressure. Avoid shaving that area until healed

• Hyperpigmentation: dark patches from repeated razor irritation. Reduce frequency of shaving

Waxing: What to Know

Waxing removes hair from the root and results last two to four weeks. It can be done at home or by a trained professional. Professional waxing in a salon reduces the risk of burns and improper technique but involves another person touching your intimate area. Ensure the salon uses clean equipment, fresh wax for each client, and sterile technique.

Waxing Cautions

• Never wax over irritated, sunburned, or broken skin

• Never wax if you have an active genital infection or rash

• Test the wax temperature on your inner arm before applying to the genital area

• The genital area skin is more sensitive than legs. Pain is more significant here

• Apply a soothing fragrance-free gel after waxing to reduce redness

• Folliculitis risk exists with waxing as well as shaving

• Avoid tight clothing for 48 hours after waxing

Hair Removal Creams: Significant Caution Required

Chemical hair removal creams work by breaking down the protein structure of hair. The chemicals required to do this are harsh and often cause severe reactions on the sensitive genital skin. Many of these products specifically state on their packaging that they should not be used in the intimate area. Chemical burns, intense irritation, and disruption of the genital skin barrier with increased infection risk are common consequences of using these creams on genital skin. If any person chooses to use them, only on the outer pubic area above the genital folds, a careful patch test on the inner thigh 24 hours before, and the shortest possible application time are essential.

Laser Hair Removal

Laser hair removal permanently reduces hair growth over multiple sessions. It requires a qualified practitioner with appropriate equipment. It is more expensive and is not suitable for all skin tones or hair colors. It is safe when performed correctly by a trained professional. The treated area must be protected from sun exposure and kept clean between sessions.

Post-Removal Care Regardless of Method

After any hair removal, the skin needs gentle care. Wear loose cotton underwear for at least 24 hours. Avoid hot baths, swimming pools, or saunas for 24 hours as they increase infection risk in open follicles. Do not use any scented products on the treated area. Do not exfoliate for 48 hours. If redness, swelling, or pus appears, this signals an infection that needs medical attention.

"No removal method is required. Every method carries risks specific to the sensitive genital skin. Choose based on your own genuine preference, with full knowledge of the risks involved."

Sanitary Pads and Common Issues

Using them correctly, understanding problems, solving them

Maryam, 18 — School student

Maryam uses sanitary pads every period but has recently started developing a rash and intense itching every month by the second day. She thinks she is allergic to something. She does not realize the issue is a combination of the wrong type of pad, changing too infrequently, and synthetic material against sensitive skin.

Sanitary pads are the most widely used menstrual product worldwide, particularly in South Asia. Using them correctly and recognizing problems they can cause prevents significant discomfort and infection.

Types of Sanitary Pads

Pads come in several sizes: panty liners for very light discharge or spotting, regular pads for moderate flow, maxi or heavy pads for heavier days, and overnight pads that are longer for use during sleep. Pads also vary in thickness, from ultra-thin to thicker cotton-feel pads. Understanding your flow and matching the right pad to the right day reduces both leaking and unnecessary bulk.

Using Sanitary Pads Correctly

• Change every 4-6 hours regardless of flow amount. Bacteria multiply rapidly in a warm, used pad

• On heavy days, change more frequently, every 2-3 hours if needed

• Always wash hands before and after changing a pad

• Place the pad centrally in the underwear with the adhesive securing it flat

• For overnight, use longer overnight pads positioned slightly further back

• Wrap used pads fully in the wrapper or toilet paper and place in a bin. Never flush

• Carry 2-3 spare pads in a clean sealed pouch whenever away from home

Common Problems With Sanitary Pads

Rash and Skin Irritation

• Cause: leaving a pad in place too long, synthetic top layer, heat and friction, fragrance in the pad

• Solution: change pads more frequently. Choose pads with a cotton or organic cotton top layer. Choose fragrance-free pads

• Prevention: apply a thin barrier of fragrance-free petroleum jelly to the skin along the pad edges if you are prone to rubbing

Allergic Reaction

• Cause: reaction to fragrances, synthetic materials, or chemical treatments in some pads

• Signs: itching, redness, small hives or bumps, burning that begins soon after using a specific brand

• Solution: switch to unscented, cotton-top, or organic cotton pads. Wash the area with cool water

• If reaction is severe or does not resolve, see a doctor

Leaking and Poor Fit

• Cause: wrong size pad for flow amount, pad not positioned correctly, pad shifting during movement

• Solution: match pad size to flow. Wear well-fitting underwear that holds the pad securely

• For active days: period underwear or menstrual cup alongside a pad as backup provides security

Odor From Used Pads

• Cause: normal menstrual blood oxidizing on a pad worn too long. Blood has no strong smell when fresh

• Solution: change pads more frequently. Odor is the body's signal that the pad has been in place too long

• Do not use scented pads to mask odor. The fragrance irritates skin and the real solution is changing more frequently

What to Look For on the Pad Packaging

Look for pads labeled fragrance-free, hypoallergenic, or with organic or natural cotton top layers if you experience skin sensitivity. Avoid pads with added deodorant or perfume. Ultra-thin pads with a completely synthetic plastic feel against the skin cause more friction and more irritation for many women. Slightly thicker cotton-feel options are gentler on sensitive skin.

When to Be Concerned

If you develop significant burning, intense itching, spreading rash, or blistering from pad use, stop using that brand immediately. If symptoms persist after switching products and changing frequently, see a doctor as you may have developed a contact dermatitis that needs treatment. Prolonged use of a saturated pad also increases risk of genital infections which need medical evaluation.

"The right pad, changed at the right time, is all that is needed for comfortable, safe period hygiene. Simplicity and frequency matter far more than brand or fragrance."

Understanding what types of injuries occur, how to respond, and when to seek immediate care is essential health knowledge.

Types of Genital Injuries in Women

Blunt Force Injuries

• Occur from impacts such as falls onto hard surfaces, bicycle crossbar impacts, sports injuries, or any direct blow

• The genital area has a rich blood supply. Even mild impacts can cause significant bruising or hematoma (blood pooling under the skin)

• A hematoma appears as rapid swelling and bruising. Small hematomas resolve with rest and ice. Large, rapidly growing hematomas need medical drainage

• Signs needing urgent care: rapidly growing swelling, inability to urinate, severe uncontrolled pain

• Occur from childbirth (perineal tears), vigorous intimate activity, hair removal accidents, falls, or sports

• Superficial tears: small surface skin breaks that cause stinging. Clean gently with water. Keep dry and clean. Usually heal within days

• Deep lacerations or tears: may involve deeper tissue, bleed significantly, or cause significant pain. Need medical evaluation and possibly stitching

• Never attempt to self-treat a significant tear

Burns

• From hot water, waxing accidents, chemical burns from hair removal creams or harsh products

• First aid: remove the irritant immediately. Flush with cool running water for at least 15-20 minutes

• Do not apply oil, butter, or toothpaste. These worsen burns

• Chemical burns from products need prompt medical attention even if initially mild

Injuries Related to Intimate Activity

• Tears of the hymenal tissue or vaginal opening can occur with first intimacy or vigorous intimate activity

• These cause pain and sometimes bleeding. Light bleeding resolves with gentle hygiene and rest

• Significant pain, heavy bleeding, or inability to urinate after intimate injury needs medical evaluation

• Bartholin gland trauma can cause painful swelling near the vaginal opening and may need medical drainage

• Any injury occurring as a result of violence or non-consensual contact requires both medical care and access to appropriate support services

For any impact or blunt trauma, apply a clean cold cloth or wrapped ice pack to the area for 15-20 minutes to reduce swelling. Do not apply ice directly to skin. Rest and avoid pressure on the area. If there is a wound or laceration, gently rinse with clean water. Apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth if bleeding. Seek medical care promptly for significant injuries.

• Heavy or persistent bleeding that does not slow with gentle pressure

• A hematoma (swelling under skin) that grows rapidly or becomes very large

• Inability to urinate after injury

• Severe pain that does not reduce within an hour of a minor injury

• Deep lacerations or tears that are gaping open

• Any injury accompanied by symptoms of shock: dizziness, faintness, very pale skin

• Any injury resulting from violence: medical care and appropriate authority reporting

• Burns covering more than a small area

Healing and Recovery

Most minor genital injuries heal well with careful hygiene, rest, and time. Keep the area clean and dry. Wear loose cotton underwear. Avoid soaking in baths until healing is complete (a day or two for minor injuries, longer for significant ones). Avoid activities that put pressure on the area until pain has resolved. Warm water sitz baths can soothe the area during healing for minor injuries.

Endometriosis is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus, called the endometrium, grows outside the uterus, typically on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and surrounding pelvic tissue. • Period pain severe enough to stop daily activities or require strong pain medicine

• Pain during or after intimacy (deep, not just surface pain)

• Pain with bowel movements or urination during periods

• Heavy periods often with clots

• Spotting between periods

• Difficulty becoming pregnant

• Fatigue particularly around the menstrual period

Ultrasound can sometimes identify endometriomas (cysts on the ovaries caused by endometriosis) but cannot detect all forms of endometriosis. Treatment options include hormonal therapies that suppress the cycle, surgical removal of endometrial tissue, and pain management. Endometriosis is a chronic condition that requires ongoing management.

• If period pain has worsened over time rather than remaining stable, see a gynaecologist

• Deep pain during intimacy combined with severe period pain needs evaluation for endometriosis

• Do not accept repeated dismissal of severe, progressive period pain as normal

The woman lies on her back with her non-dominant arm bent at the elbow. The inner upper arm is cleaned carefully. The doctor gives a small injection of local anaesthetic into the skin at the insertion point. This stings briefly but numbs the area within one to two minutes. The woman will feel pressure but not pain after this.

Using a special sterile applicator that looks like a thick pen, the doctor inserts the implant just beneath the skin. The whole procedure takes less than one minute. A small plaster is placed over the tiny insertion point. There is no stitching needed. The rod can be felt under the skin with the fingers but is not visible from outside.

• The arm may feel sore, bruised, or tender for a few days — this is normal

• There may be some swelling and bruising around the insertion site that fades within one to two weeks

• The small plaster underneath can be removed after three to five days

• You can feel the implant under the skin — check that it is there by gently pressing the area

• Keep the area clean and dry for the first 24-48 hours

• Avoid heavy lifting or vigorous use of that arm for two to three days

• Do not press or massage the insertion site for the first week

• Normal bathing and swimming are fine after the first 24 hours

• Wear loose-sleeved clothing for the first few days if the arm is sore

• Mild pain relievers like paracetamol help if the arm feels tender

• The contraceptive effect begins immediately if inserted in the first five days of the period

• Some women have more frequent or unpredictable spotting

• Irregular periods settle for most women within the first year

• The implant cannot be felt after insertion — this is rare but needs urgent review

• Severe arm pain, numbness, or tingling needs evaluation

• Pregnancy symptoms while using the implant need an immediate test and review

The progestogen in the implant suppresses the LH surge that triggers ovulation. Without the LH surge, the ovary does not release an egg. The woman lies on her back with her knees bent and legs apart, similar to a standard gynaecological examination. The doctor gently inserts a speculum into the vaginal opening to see the cervix. The cervix and vaginal walls are cleaned with antiseptic solution.

The IUCD is then folded inside a thin sterile tube called an inserter. The inserter is passed through the cervical opening into the uterus. When the inserter reaches the correct position, the IUCD opens into its T-shape inside the uterus. The inserter is gently withdrawn, leaving the IUCD in place with two thin nylon threads hanging just below the cervix into the upper vaginal canal.

The threads allow the woman to check the IUCD is in place and allow the doctor to remove it when needed. The entire insertion process takes approximately five minutes.

• The speculum insertion feels like pressure

• Some women feel dizzy or lightheaded briefly after insertion — rest is offered before leaving

• Taking a mild pain reliever like ibuprofen one to two hours before the appointment helps significantly

• Cramping and light spotting for two to three days after insertion are normal

• A sanitary pad is useful for the first few days — avoid tampons for the first 48 hours

• Avoid strenuous exercise for two to three days

After the general anaesthetic takes effect, the surgeon makes a very small cut of about one centimetre just below or inside the navel. A thin needle is used to fill the abdomen with carbon dioxide gas. This gas gently lifts the abdominal wall away from the organs inside, creating a clear space to work in.

The laparoscope, which is a thin tube with a tiny camera and light source at its end, is inserted through the navel cut. The surgeon views the entire pelvis on a screen — the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and surrounding structures. If endometriosis, adhesions, cysts, or other abnormalities are found, a tissue sample may be taken or, if appropriate, the condition may be treated during the same procedure. One to two additional very small cuts of 5 millimetres may be made for instrument insertion during treatment.

At the end of the procedure, the gas is released, the instruments are removed, and the small cuts are closed with one or two absorbable stitches or adhesive strips. The entire procedure typically takes 30 minutes to one hour.

What Happens Before the Procedure

• No food or water from midnight before the procedure (fasting instructions given by the hospital)

• Any regular medicines are reviewed by the doctor — some are continued, some paused

• Blood tests and sometimes a urine pregnancy test are done before surgery

• A consent form explaining the procedure, its risks, and benefits is signed

• Comfortable, loose clothing for coming home is recommended

• Arrange for someone to drive you home — you cannot drive after general anaesthesia

Waking Up After the Procedure

After the procedure, the woman wakes up in the recovery area. There may be some groggy feeling from the anaesthetic that clears over one to two hours. The small cuts will feel sore. The most common unexpected discomfort after laparoscopy is shoulder tip pain, which feels like aching in the shoulder area. This happens because the carbon dioxide gas used during the procedure irritates the diaphragm and the pain is referred up to the shoulder. It is not a shoulder problem and resolves within 24-48 hours.

Care After Diagnostic Laparoscopy

• Rest for the remainder of the day after the procedure. Most women go home the same day

• Shoulder tip pain: walk around gently, apply warm compress to shoulder area, takes 24-48 hours to resolve

• Bloating and mild abdominal discomfort from the gas: walking helps clear it faster

• Keep the small wound sites clean and dry for the first 24-48 hours

• Gentle showering is fine after 24 hours — avoid soaking baths until wounds are healed

• Mild pain relievers (paracetamol and ibuprofen together if prescribed) manage wound discomfort

• Light activities can resume after 48-72 hours

• Return to desk work within three to five days for most women

• Avoid heavy lifting, strenuous exercise, and driving for one week

• Avoid penetrative intimacy for two to four weeks or until the follow-up appointment

• Wound check or follow-up appointment is usually one to two weeks after the procedure

WHEN TO SEE A DOCTOR

• Fever above 38 degrees C after the procedure — suggests infection

• Increasing rather than decreasing pain in the abdomen in the days after surgery

• Redness, swelling, or discharge from any wound site

• Heavy vaginal bleeding after the procedure

• Difficulty urinating or passing urine with burning

• Severe shoulder pain lasting more than 48 hours

WHAT SCIENCE SAYS · Why Laparoscopy Is Better Than Open Surgery for Diagnosis

Laparoscopy uses cuts of 5-10mm compared to the large cuts of open surgery. Recovery time is significantly shorter. Pain is less. The risk of infection and complications is lower. The view through the laparoscope is often magnified and clearer than the view through a large open incision. For investigation of pelvic conditions, laparoscopy has become the gold standard.

"A diagnostic laparoscopy is a keyhole procedure, not major open surgery. The cuts are tiny. Recovery is measured in days rather than weeks. The information it provides can explain years of unexplained pain and guide treatment directly."

Chapter P4

Nabothian Cysts — What They Are and When They Need Treatment

Tiny cervical cysts, simply explained

Sunita, 29 — Married

During a routine gynaecology checkup, Sunita's doctor mentions she has Nabothian cysts on her cervix. Sunita has never heard this term and immediately worries it means something serious. The doctor explains that they are extremely common and almost always harmless.

Nabothian cysts are small, benign (harmless) fluid-filled sacs that form on the surface of the cervix. They develop when the mucus-producing glands of the cervix become blocked, often after the squamocolumnar junction (the area where two types of cervical cells meet) shifts, covering the gland openings. They look like small, smooth, white or yellowish lumps on the cervix surface.

Nabothian cysts are extremely common. Many women have them without knowing. They are almost always discovered incidentally during a routine gynaecological examination or cervical scan. They cause no symptoms in the vast majority of cases and require no treatment.

When Do Nabothian Cysts Need Treatment?

The great majority of Nabothian cysts need no treatment at all. A doctor may choose to observe them over time with periodic checks. Treatment is only considered when the cysts are unusually large, causing symptoms such as discharge or discomfort, or when the doctor wants to see the cervical tissue beneath them more clearly for diagnostic purposes.

What Happens During Treatment (Incision or Ablation)

When treatment is needed, the procedure is straightforward and usually performed in the outpatient clinic without general anaesthesia. The woman lies in the same position as a standard gynaecological examination. The speculum is inserted to see the cervix. The cervix is cleaned with antiseptic solution.

Depending on the method used, the doctor may pierce or incise the cyst with a fine sterile needle or small instrument to release the fluid inside. Alternatively, cryotherapy (freezing), electrocautery (a tiny electrical current), or laser ablation may be used to destroy the blocked gland. The procedure takes only a few minutes. A local anaesthetic may be applied to the cervix beforehand. Most women feel mild cramping or pressure during the procedure.

What to Expect During the Procedure

• Position: lying on the examination table as for a standard gynaec exam

• Duration: five to fifteen minutes

• Sensation: mild cramping or pressure, similar to a smear test

• Anaesthetic: local anaesthetic spray or injection to the cervix in many cases

• A small amount of discharge or fluid release when the cyst is drained

• Minimal discomfort immediately afterwards

Care After Nabothian Cyst Treatment

After-Procedure Care

• Mild cramping for a few hours after the procedure is normal — paracetamol helps

• A small amount of watery or light discharge for several days is expected as the cervix heals

• Use a sanitary pad for the first few days — avoid tampons until the follow-up

• Normal daily activities including desk work can resume the same or next day

• Avoid penetrative intimacy for two to four weeks to allow cervical healing

• Avoid swimming and soaking baths for two to three weeks

• Avoid strenuous exercise for one week

• A follow-up appointment is typically scheduled at four to six weeks

WHEN TO SEE A DOCTOR

• Heavy bleeding, more than a normal period flow, after the procedure

• Fever or increasing lower abdominal pain suggesting infection

• Foul-smelling discharge after the procedure

• Discharge continuing beyond three to four weeks

"Nabothian cysts are one of the most common and most harmless cervical findings. Most need no treatment. When treatment is needed, the procedure is brief, low-risk, and performed in a clinic setting."

Chapter P5

Episiotomy After Delivery — What It Is and How to Heal

A cut made to help delivery — and how to recover from it gently

Priya, 28 — New mother, first baby

Priya has just delivered her first baby vaginally. During the delivery, the midwife told her she was giving her an episiotomy. Priya heard the word but was focused on her baby. Now, two days after delivery, she has significant pain in the perineum and wants to understand what was done and how to care for it.

An episiotomy is a small surgical cut made in the perineum — the area of muscle and skin between the vaginal opening and the anus — during the final stage of vaginal delivery. It is made by the midwife or obstetrician when additional space is needed for the baby to be born safely, when the delivery needs to happen quickly for medical reasons, or when the perineal skin appears likely to tear in an uncontrolled way.

Why Is an Episiotomy Done?

The most common reasons are when the baby's head is large relative to the vaginal opening, when the baby shows signs of distress and rapid delivery is needed, when the use of forceps or vacuum delivery is required (these instruments need space), when the mother has difficulty pushing the baby out effectively, and when a natural tear is beginning in a direction that could cause more damage than a controlled cut.

What Happens During the Episiotomy

At the point in delivery when the baby's head is visible at the vaginal opening, the skin and muscle of the perineum are stretched very tight. At this moment, because the pressure itself provides some natural numbing, a local anaesthetic injection is given. The midwife or doctor then makes a single clean, angled cut of approximately three to four centimetres using sterile scissors. This enlarges the vaginal opening so the baby can be born.

Immediately after the baby and placenta are delivered, the cut is repaired by suturing (stitching) in layers. The muscle layer beneath is sutured first, then the skin is closed with absorbable stitches that dissolve on their own over two to three weeks. The suturing typically takes fifteen to twenty minutes and is done under continued local anaesthetic so the mother feels only pressure, not pain.

Types of Episiotomy Cuts

• Mediolateral episiotomy: cut at an angle away from the midline, most commonly used in many countries including India. Avoids the anal sphincter.

• Median or midline episiotomy: cut straight back toward the anus. Heals more easily but carries a higher risk of extending to the anal sphincter.

• The midwife or doctor chooses the type based on anatomy and the specific delivery situation.

Pain and the First Days After Episiotomy

Pain in the perineal area after an episiotomy is normal and expected. It is typically most significant in the first two to four days and then gradually improves over the following weeks. The area feels sore, bruised, and sometimes swollen. Sitting may be uncomfortable. Walking may feel tender. Passing urine may cause stinging as urine contacts the wound — pouring warm water over the area while urinating reduces this.

Perineal Care After Episiotomy — The Essentials

• Keep the area clean: gently rinse with warm water from a jug or squeeze bottle after every toilet visit

• Pat dry gently with clean soft tissue or a clean cloth — always from front to back

• Change maternity pads every two to four hours — blood and discharge from the wound make a clean environment essential

• Sitz bath: sitting in a shallow warm bath for ten to fifteen minutes two to three times daily significantly reduces pain and promotes healing

• Ice pack for the first 24-48 hours: wrapped in a thin cloth, applied for fifteen minutes several times a day, reduces swelling markedly

• Pain relief: regular paracetamol and ibuprofen (if not breastfeeding contraindicated) manage pain very effectively — take regularly, not only when pain is severe

• Wear loose cotton underwear that does not press on the wound

• High-fibre diet and plenty of water to ensure soft, easy bowel movements — straining during bowel movements causes significant pain and risks wound breakdown

• Pelvic floor exercises (Kegel exercises): begin very gently within 24-48 hours of delivery to improve blood flow to the area and support healing

When Healing Is Going Well

• Pain gradually decreasing each day after the third day

• Stitches not visible as separate threads — they dissolve and merge with the healing tissue

• Wound edges coming together, not gaping

• No foul smell from the wound area

• Normal lochia (postpartum vaginal discharge) separate from any wound discharge

• Ability to sit more comfortably by one to two weeks

• Most women feel comfortable enough to return to gentle activity by four to six weeks

WHEN TO SEE A DOCTOR

• Increasing rather than decreasing pain after the third day

• Wound that appears to be opening or gaping

• Redness, heat, or pus from the wound site — signs of infection

• Fever above 38 degrees C after delivery

• Inability to pass urine or complete incontinence of urine or faeces

• Bleeding significantly more than a normal period from the wound site

• A hard or very painful lump developing near the wound suggests haematoma

Returning to Intimacy After Episiotomy

Most medical guidelines suggest waiting at least six weeks after delivery before resuming penetrative intimacy, and longer if the episiotomy wound is still tender or healing is slow. Emotional readiness, physical comfort, and adequate lubrication (which may be reduced during breastfeeding due to low estrogen) all matter. Water-based lubricant is helpful. Communication with a partner about comfort levels is essential. Any pain during intimacy after the recommended waiting period should be discussed with the doctor rather than endured.

WHAT SCIENCE SAYS · Why Episiotomy Wounds Sometimes Feel Like They Are Healing Slowly

The perineum has a very high nerve density, which is why even small wounds in this area produce significant pain. However, it also has very good blood supply, which means healing is actually faster than in many other areas. The dissolving stitches may cause mild itching as they dissolve, which is a sign of healing, not infection. Full tissue strength is restored over several months even when surface healing appears complete.

"An episiotomy is a procedure done for the safety of you and your baby. The wound heals completely. Recovery requires patience, consistent gentle care, and proper pain management. Most women feel significantly better within two weeks and comfortable by six weeks."

Emergency Red Flags — Quick Reference Card

Symptoms that need immediate or same-day medical attention.

GO TO EMERGENCY IMMEDIATELY FOR:

• Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain (possible ectopic pregnancy or ovarian torsion)

• Vaginal bleeding soaking more than one pad per hour for two consecutive hours

• Positive pregnancy test with one-sided pain and dizziness

• Fever with severe pelvic pain and unwell appearance

• Genital injury with heavy uncontrolled bleeding

• Sudden inability to urinate after delivery or pelvic injury

• Signs of severe infection: high fever, confusion, rapid breathing, and pelvic pain

SEE A DOCTOR SAME DAY FOR:

• Heavy vaginal bleeding that is new and not the normal period

• Fever above 38°C with any gynaecological symptom

• Rapidly growing swelling in the genital or pelvic area

• Wound (episiotomy, caesarean, post-procedure) showing redness, pus, or widening gap

• Inability to pass urine for more than 8 hours after surgery

• Severe headache with visual changes after delivery

BOOK A DOCTOR APPOINTMENT WITHIN ONE WEEK FOR:

• Any new lump in the breast, genitals, or pelvis

• Discharge that has changed color, smell, or consistency

• Pain during intimate activity that is new or worsening

• Periods that have significantly changed without obvious cause

• Symptoms of a urinary tract infection that have not improved after 48 hours

• Mood symptoms severe enough to affect work or relationships before periods

APPENDIX I

Common Medicines in Women's Health — Simply Explained

What common medicines are prescribed for, and what to remember when taking them.

MEDICINE

COMMONLY USED FOR

IMPORTANT POINTS

Iron tablets (Ferrous sulphate / fumarate)

Iron deficiency anaemia

Take on an empty stomach for best absorption. Take with vitamin C (amla, orange juice) to improve absorption. Avoid with tea, coffee, or calcium within 2 hours. Causes dark stools — this is harmless. May cause constipation — increase water and fibre intake.

Folic Acid (Folate / Vitamin B9)

Pregnancy prevention of neural tube defects. Also prescribed in anaemia.

Start at least 3 months before trying to conceive. Continue for the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Safe and important.

Vitamin D supplements

Vitamin D deficiency

Dose depends on blood level — do not self-prescribe high doses. Vitamin D is fat-soluble: take with a meal containing fat for best absorption. Recheck levels after 3 months of supplementation.

Metformin

PCOS, insulin resistance, prediabetes

Take with food to reduce nausea. Start with a low dose. Common side effects: nausea, loose stools in the beginning (usually settles). Rarely causes lactic acidosis — report muscle pain or weakness immediately.

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill

Contraception, period regulation, PCOS, endometriosis

Take at the same time every day. Does not protect against STIs. May cause nausea in the first month. Stop if you develop severe headaches, vision changes, or leg pain and seek urgent care.

Progesterone-only (mini) Pill

Contraception, especially during breastfeeding

Take at the same time every day — even a 3-hour delay reduces effectiveness of some types. Periods may become irregular.

Levonorgestrel (Emergency Pill)

Emergency contraception after unprotected intimacy

Must be taken within 72 hours (earlier is more effective). Not for regular use. May cause nausea. Next period may be early or late.

Mefenamic Acid / Ibuprofen

Painful periods (dysmenorrhoea)

Take at the first sign of period pain — earlier is more effective. Always take with food. Avoid with peptic ulcer history. Not suitable for long-term daily use.

Tranexamic Acid

Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia)

Reduces bleeding by helping blood clot. Take only during the period, not throughout the month. Does not affect hormones.

Thyroid tablets (Levothyroxine)

Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)

Take on an empty stomach first thing in the morning, 30-60 minutes before food. Do not take with calcium, iron, or dairy within 2 hours. Dose adjusted based on TSH blood tests.

Antifungal cream/tablet (Fluconazole / Clotrimazole)

Genital yeast infection

Oral tablet for systemic treatment, cream for local symptom relief. Complete the full course. Avoid during first trimester of pregnancy — oral type especially.

Metronidazole

Bacterial vaginosis, Trichomonas infection

Complete full course even if symptoms resolve. Avoid alcohol completely during treatment and for 48 hours after. Partner may need treatment simultaneously.

SSRIs (e.g. Sertraline, Fluoxetine)

PMDD, depression, anxiety

May take 2-4 weeks to feel the full benefit. Do not stop suddenly — taper under doctor guidance. Discuss with doctor before stopping if planning pregnancy.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine without consulting your doctor. Never take someone else's prescription. If you experience an unexpected reaction to any medicine, stop taking it and contact your doctor or go to a pharmacy immediately.

APPENDIX J

Pelvic Floor Exercises — Step-by-Step Guide

Simple exercises for bladder control, recovery after delivery, and long-term pelvic health.

The pelvic floor is a group of muscles at the base of the pelvis. These muscles support the bladder, bowel, and uterus. They are involved in bladder and bowel control, sexual comfort, and support during pregnancy and delivery. Like all muscles, they can be strengthened through regular, correct exercise.

STEP 1 Find the right muscles

Sit or lie comfortably. Imagine you are trying to stop yourself urinating mid-flow. The muscles that squeeze and lift inward are the pelvic floor muscles. Do not squeeze the buttocks, thighs, or abdomen — only the pelvic floor. You should feel a lift and squeeze inside.

STEP 2 Slow squeeze and hold

Squeeze and lift the pelvic floor muscles gently. Hold for 3 seconds. Release slowly and completely. This is one repetition. Rest for 3 seconds between each repetition.

STEP 3 Build the hold gradually

Over two weeks, increase the hold time to 5 seconds, then 8 seconds, then 10 seconds. The goal is a sustained, controlled squeeze — not a very tight, short squeeze.

STEP 4 Quick contractions

After the slow holds, do 10 fast, strong contractions — squeeze and release quickly, 1 second on and 1 second off. This trains the muscles for responses like coughing and sneezing.

STEP 5 Complete a set

10 slow holds + 10 fast contractions = 1 set.

STEP 6 Frequency

3 sets per day. This can be done anywhere — sitting, standing, or lying down. No equipment needed. No one can see you doing it.

STEP 7 Consistency over intensity

Daily practice for 8-12 weeks produces noticeable improvement. Most women notice better bladder control and reduced leakage within 4-6 weeks of consistent practice.

WHO ESPECIALLY BENEFITS: Women who leak urine when they cough, sneeze, laugh or exercise. Women after vaginal delivery. Women preparing for vaginal delivery. Women with pelvic heaviness. Women with reduced intimate sensation. ALL women benefit from regular pelvic floor exercise as a long-term investment in bladder and pelvic health.
